0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
To the southeast of Anjou, a tributary flows from south to north into the Loire — the Layon. In autumn it brings regular morning mists, creating the cradle of western France's greatest botrytised sweet wines. From entry-level Coteaux du Layon to the top Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, the whole sweet-wine pyramid is built on Chenin Blanc + Botrytis cinerea + a mixed terroir of tuffeau and schist.

Learning Objectives

🍄 The Botrytis cinerea mechanism

Understand how noble rot penetrates the grape skin, concentrates sugar and acidity, and generates glycerol and distinctive flavour compounds

🏔️ The Layon sweet-wine pyramid

The tiering logic from Coteaux du Layon → Coteaux du Layon Villages → Bonnezeaux → Quarts de Chaume GC

🌫️ Microclimate conditions

Grasp the Layon valley's "golden conditions for noble rot": morning mist + dry afternoons

🏆 Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru

Get to know the Loire's only Grand Cru AOC (recognised in 2011) and its strict regulations
1.title: The Layon Valley — Western France's Noble-Rot Paradise
1.highlights.0.title: Morning mist triggers noble rot
1.highlights.0.content: The Layon valley is narrow and runs northwest–southeast; on autumn mornings it generates thick mist (high humidity)
1.highlights.1.title: Dry afternoons
1.highlights.1.content: After the mist clears, south-facing slopes get full sun, suppressing harmful grey rot and promoting healthy noble rot
1.highlights.2.title: Schist terroir
1.highlights.2.content: Black schist of the Anjou Noir + tuffeau lend the sweet wines mineral tension and keep them from being merely cloying
1.content:
The Layon is a left-bank tributary of the Loire, flowing north from Vihiers to Chalonnes-sur-Loire, about 90 km in total. The vineyards lie mainly on south-facing slopes on the north bank of the valley; this distinctive landform lets the morning mist build up and then clear completely in the afternoon — precisely the golden conditions for noble rot.

🌫️ The three elements of golden noble-rot conditions

  1. High humidity in the early morning: moisture from the Layon evaporates before sunrise and gathers at the foot of the slopes, producing thick mist. Mist humidity of 90%+ supplies the moisture for Botrytis cinerea spores to germinate
  2. Hot, dry afternoons: the mist lifts at 10–11 am and south-facing slopes warm quickly to 20°C+. The dry conditions stop Botrytis turning from "noble rot" into "grey rot"
  3. Successive picking (Tries Successives): grapes are not infected by noble rot all at once, so pickers must return to the same vineyard several times, selecting only bunches or berries that have reached the "pourriture noble" state

🪨 Layon soils

Unlike Vouvray's pure tuffeau, the Layon lies in the Anjou Noir (Black Anjou) zone:

  • Schist: the main parent rock, black-grey, friable, rich in organic matter
  • Tuffeau: on the margins, similar to Vouvray
  • Sandy soil: river-terrace alluvium with excellent drainage

The key role of schist: it retains high acidity and adds flint/graphite mineral texture, balancing the sweetness brought by Botrytis.
1.quiz.question: What is the key microclimate for noble-rot development in the Layon valley?
1.quiz.options.1: Daily variation of high morning humidity and dry afternoons
1.quiz.explanation: Botrytis cinerea noble rot needs a "wet → dry → wet → dry" cycle. The Layon valley's narrow, northwest–southeast landform produces thick mist every autumn morning (high humidity triggers the spores) and dry afternoons after the mist clears (suppressing harmful grey rot and concentrating the grapes). This daily rhythm matters more than humidity alone — if it were damp all day, the grapes would simply rot.

3.title: The Layon Sweet-Wine Pyramid
3.highlights.0.content: The Loire's only Grand Cru, regulations passed in 2011 (applicable from the 2010 vintage), about 40 hectares
3.highlights.1.content: A single Cru AOC, about 80–120 hectares (sources vary), a historic vineyard on a par with QdC
3.highlights.2.content: 6 designated villages: Beaulieu, Faye, Rablay, Rochefort, Saint-Aubin, Saint-Lambert; Chaume stands apart as a Premier Cru
3.content:
The Layon sweet-wine system is one of the most complex sweet-wine classifications in France. From entry to top level it divides into 4 tiers, and with each step up the minimum residual sugar, maximum yield and grape-ripeness requirements all become stricter.

🥇 Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru (the Loire's only GC)

  • Area: about 40 hectares, in the village of Rochefort-sur-Loire
  • Maximum yield: 20 hL/ha (the strictest)
  • Sugar threshold: must sugar ≥ 298 g/L, residual sugar after fermentation > 85 g/L (Botrytis infection must be high)
  • Harvest: must be by hand, in multiple passes (par tries successives)
  • Top names: Château de Bellerive, Château Pierre-Bise, Domaine des Baumard
  • History: the name comes from the 15th-century feudal-tax story of "the best quarter"

🥈 Bonnezeaux (single Cru AOC)

  • Area: about 80–120 hectares (sources vary), in the village of Thouarcé
  • Maximum yield: 25 hL/ha
  • Minimum residual sugar: 51 g/L (Moelleux level and above; must sugar ≥ 238 g/L)
  • Three main slopes: La Montagne, Beauregard, Fesles (plus other plot names such as Les Melleresses)
  • Top names: Château de Fesles, Domaine Petit Val, Domaine des Petits Quarts

🥉 Coteaux du Layon Villages (6 designated villages)

  • Area: about 200 hectares
  • Maximum yield: 30 hL/ha
  • Minimum residual sugar: 34 g/L (must sugar ≥ 238 g/L, alcohol ≥ 12%)
  • The 6 villages: Beaulieu-sur-Layon, Faye-d'Anjou, Rablay-sur-Layon, Rochefort-sur-Loire, Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné, Saint-Lambert-du-Lattay; Chaume Premier Cru, within the commune of Rochefort, is a separate AOC (about 80 hectares, must sugar ≥ 272 g/L, 25 hL/ha)

📦 Coteaux du Layon (base AOC)

  • Area: about 1,400 hectares, across 27 villages
  • Maximum yield: 35 hL/ha
  • Minimum residual sugar: 34 g/L (Demi-sec and above; must sugar ≥ 221 g/L)
  • Position: entry-level noble-rot wine, offering good value
3.quiz.question: What is Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru's special status in the Loire?
3.quiz.options.1: The Loire's only Grand Cru AOC (recognised in 2011)
3.quiz.explanation: In 2011 (applicable from the 2010 vintage), Quarts de Chaume was promoted from its original AOC status to become the only "Grand Cru" AOC in the Loire Valley (the other Grand Crus in France, such as those of Alsace, Burgundy and Chablis, each have their own systems). This small area of about 40 hectares sits in the naturally sheltered landform of a Layon tributary, where autumn noble-rot conditions are extremely stable.
4.title: Botrytis cinerea — The Chemical Magic of Noble Rot
4.highlights.0.title: Hyphae penetrate the skin
4.highlights.0.content: Enzymes secreted through the waxy layer of the skin create a "micro-pore effect," while the skin as a whole stays intact
4.highlights.1.title: Water evaporation
4.highlights.1.content: The micro-pores let the grape's water evaporate slowly, concentrating sugar, acid and aroma precursors 2–3 times
4.highlights.2.title: Glycerol + flavour compounds
4.highlights.2.content: Generates large amounts of glycerol (rounded mouthfeel) and sotolon (honey, curry, nuts)
4.content:
Botrytis cinerea is a filamentous fungus. In "bad" conditions it rots grapes outright (grey rot), causing heavy losses; but in "good" conditions (morning mist + dry afternoons) it slowly transforms grapes as "noble rot" (pourriture noble), creating the legend of sweet wine.

🔬 Five stages of noble rot

  1. Spore attachment: mist brings moisture and spores germinate on the grape skin
  2. Hyphal penetration: hyphae secrete enzymes into the skin, forming micro-pores without destroying the skin's overall integrity
  3. Micro-pore formation: the enzymes partly dissolve the skin, creating micro-pore channels
  4. Water evaporation: in dry afternoon conditions, water evaporates slowly through the pores, concentrating sugar from 22°Brix to 35–45°Brix
  5. Grape shrivelling: the berries turn pinkish-purple and shrivel like raisins, known as "pourri plein" (perfect noble rot)

🧪 Characteristic compounds of noble rot

  • Glycerol: 5–25 g/L (ordinary wine has only 5–8 g/L), giving an oily, silky mouthfeel
  • Gluconic acid: the signature by-product of noble rot, which analysis can use to confirm infection
  • Sotolon: a key flavour compound — honey, curry, fenugreek, nuts, maple syrup aromas
  • Phenylacetaldehyde: rose and violet floral notes
  • Sugar: 200–300+ g/L, with high residual sugar kept after fermentation
4.quiz.question: Which of the following does Botrytis cinerea **not** do during noble rot?
4.quiz.options.0: Penetrate the skin with enzymes and form micro-pores
4.quiz.options.2: Completely destroy the skin so the juice flows out
4.quiz.explanation: Noble-rot Botrytis does not destroy the overall structure of the skin — it only secretes enzymes to form micro-pores that let water evaporate slowly. Once the skin is completely broken down (for example by rain or clumping), it becomes harmful "grey rot," and the whole batch of grapes has to be discarded. This is why the Layon's dry afternoons are so critical: they keep Botrytis at the "noble rot" stage.
5.title: Level 3-3 Knowledge Check
5.questions.0.question: What is the minimum residual sugar requirement for Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru?
5.questions.0.explanation: The Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru regulations require residual sugar after fermentation > 85 g/L (must sugar at least 298 g/L), one of the strictest rules among Loire sweet wines. The maximum yield is also the strictest (20 hL/ha), ensuring the grapes reach ultimate noble-rot concentration.
5.questions.1.question: What is the core grape variety of Layon sweet wines?
5.questions.1.explanation: All of the Layon's noble-rot sweet AOCs (Coteaux du Layon, Bonnezeaux, Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru) require 100% Chenin Blanc. Chenin's high natural acidity (pH 3.0–3.2) stays balanced even after heavy noble rot, preventing the sweet wines from being cloying — which is why it ranks alongside Sémillon (Sauternes) as one of the two great noble-rot varieties.
5.questions.2.question: Why do Layon sweet wines usually seem lighter than Sauternes?
5.questions.2.options.1: Chenin Blanc's natural acidity is higher than Sémillon's, balancing the sweetness
5.questions.2.explanation: The essential difference between Layon (Chenin) and Sauternes (Sémillon + Sauvignon) is varietal acidity. Chenin Blanc's pH is usually 3.0–3.2 (very high acidity), so even with 100+ g/L residual sugar it shows tension and freshness. Sémillon's pH is usually 3.3–3.6, and with Sauternes' higher alcohol (13–14% vs Layon's 10–12%), the overall palate is thicker and fuller.
5.questions.3.question: What is the purpose of Tries Successives (successive picking)?
5.questions.3.options.1: To pick, at different times, only the bunches or berries that have reached perfect noble rot
5.questions.3.explanation: Botrytis does not infect a whole vineyard at once — within the same bunch, some berries may already be perfectly botrytised while others are not yet infected or have only just begun. Tries Successives requires pickers to return to the vineyard several times (at least 3 times for top QdC GC, and 6–8 times at some estates), each time picking only the berries that have reached the "pourri plein" state. The labour cost is extremely high, but it guarantees the quality of top noble-rot wines.
5.questions.4.question: How many villages may appear on a Coteaux du Layon Villages label, and what is Chaume's status?
5.questions.4.options.1: 6, with Chaume a separate Premier Cru (within Rochefort)
5.questions.4.explanation: Villages designates 6 villages (Beaulieu, Faye, Rablay, Rochefort, Saint-Aubin, Saint-Lambert), with must sugar ≥ 238 g/L. Chaume is a plot within Rochefort-sur-Loire and is a separate Coteaux du Layon Premier Cru Chaume (about 80 hectares, must sugar ≥ 272 g/L, 25 hL/ha). Quarts de Chaume is the Grand Cru.
